title: Chayei Sarah: the servant's prayer (Genesis 24:12–15)
hookLine: before he finishes praying, Rebekah comes out with her jar

cards: Abraham, old now, calls in his servant, the elder of his house, who runs everything he owns, and hands him a job way above anyone's pay grade: go back to my homeland and find a wife for my son Isaac. No address. No photo.
No app. The servant loads ten camels and makes the long trip. He arrives at evening, at a well outside the city, at the hour the women come out to draw water.
He makes the camels kneel. And before doing anything else, he talks to God.

teach.b: The servant isn't named in this chapter; tradition often calls him Eliezer, from earlier in Genesis.
His prayer, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, begins: "O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, send me, I pray Thee, good speed this day, and show kindness unto my master Abraham."
Notice how ordinary it is. No grand titles, no long speech. Just: please, today, help.
Then he gets specific. I'm standing by the well. The young women are coming out.
Let the one I ask for a drink say: drink, and I'll water your camels too. Let her be the one. That's a big ask.
Ten thirsty camels drink a lot of water, and the jar has to go down to the spring and up again, many times. He isn't asking for a pretty face. He's asking for someone kind past what's required.

Then this line: "before he had done speaking," Rebekah comes out with her jar on her shoulder. He runs to meet her. She gives him a drink and says, I'll draw for your camels too, until they've finished.
She runs back and forth to the well while he stands there, silent, watching, wondering if this is really happening.
Some readers find the request bold, and the Talmud counts it among requests made improperly, since the wrong woman could have answered.
Still, some teachers hold up the prayer itself as a model: short, plain, naming what he needs.
Jewish tradition has room for long, formal prayers, and also for this: a person, tired from the road, telling God what they need, in their own words.

how: Alongside the set prayers of the prayer book, Jewish tradition welcomes personal prayer in one's own words and language, and some add their own requests within the Amidah, the central standing prayer.

games.why: he made the camels kneel and prayed a short, plain prayer. before he had finished speaking, Rebekah came out.

practice: Think of one thing you need help with right now, not a wish list, just one, and say it in one short sentence, as plain as the servant's: help me with this, today.
If you pray, say it to God; if you don't, say it to yourself, or plan to say it to a person who could help. Then breathe, and wait, the way he stood by the well.
